findings.title: Video-embed wrapper made an injected callable, which legitimises autoevolution's missing YouTube host allowlist
findings.description:
Decision 1 names the video-embed wrapper as one of three per-site injected callables. Neither Decision 1 nor any other section states the contract that an injected wrapper MUST apply a hostname allowlist BEFORE running the video-ID regex.

orangetrack_source.py:138-169 gets this right and its docstring names the exact gap it was written to close: 'The hostname allowlist gate runs BEFORE the ID regex - without it, a non-YouTube URL containing the substring youtube.com/embed/abc would be falsely wrapped (autoevolution's regex-only path has this gap; we close it here per Decision 8).' It parses the URL, checks host in _YOUTUBE_HOSTS (7 entries), and only then searches _YOUTUBE_ID_RE.

autoevolution_source.py:106-124 IS that regex-only path. It runs YOUTUBE_ID_RE.search(href) and VIMEO_ID_RE.search(href) directly on the raw scraped href with no urlparse, no host check, and a Vimeo branch orangetrack does not have. Its call site (autoevolution_source.py:264-272) feeds it every <a href> in the article body.

Task 7 says only that autoevolution's _runs_from_tag is replaced by the shared walker and that 'its block/lead/heading structure already exists and must keep working'. _video_embed_url is never mentioned. So the plan preserves the vulnerable wrapper verbatim and, worse, promotes it from an acknowledged defect into a sanctioned injection value that the shared module accepts without validation. A future fifth source copying autoevolution's call pattern inherits the gap silently, which is precisely the outcome user-spec Risk 1 ('перенос кода вместе с его багами') and Decision 1's own rationale ('the next such bug is fixed once, not four times') exist to prevent.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 1 (injected callables); Task 7; autoevolution_source.py:33-37, 106-124, 264-272 vs orangetrack_source.py:49-60, 88-91, 138-169
findings.impact: Any party who can influence autoevolution article HTML (compromised CMS, injected comment/ad markup, feed tampering, or an open redirect on their domain) can place a link such as https://attacker.example/track?u=youtube.com/embed/<id> and have the bot emit a {'type':'video','src':'https://telegra.ph/embed/youtube?url=...'} block. That iframe is published to the Telegraph page and pushed to the Telegram channel via Instant View, so arbitrary third-party video is attributed to the channel - a content-integrity and reputational compromise of the published artifact. The Vimeo branch doubles the provider surface with the same gap. Compounding the same code path: both ID captures are open-ended ([A-Za-z0-9_-]+ in autoevolution, [A-Za-z0-9_-]{6,} in orangetrack), so a multi-megabyte href yields a multi-megabyte 'video ID' that is percent-encoded (roughly 3x expansion), stored in the blocks JSON in SQLite, and carried into the Telegraph createPage payload. Because the spec's whole architectural claim is that shared code fixes a class of bug once, shipping the extraction with the weaker wrapper injected makes the security posture strictly worse than today: the gap acquires an interface.
findings.recommendation:
Amend Decision 1 to state the invariant, and amend Task 7 to carry it out:

1. dom_blocks.py owns ONE video-embed implementation with the gate built in, and per-site injection supplies only DATA (an allowed-host tuple plus a provider name), never the whole callable:

   def video_embed_url(url, *, allowed_hosts, provider, id_re):
       if not isinstance(url, str) or not url:
           return None
       try:
           host = (urlparse(url).hostname or '').lower()
       except (ValueError, AttributeError):
           return None
       if host not in allowed_hosts:      # gate FIRST, always
           return None
       m = id_re.search(url)
       if not m:
           return None
       vid = m.group(1)
       if len(vid) > 64:                  # bound the capture
           return None
       ...

2. Give Vimeo the same treatment autoevolution never had: _VIMEO_HOSTS = ('vimeo.com', 'www.vimeo.com', 'player.vimeo.com').

3. Bound both ID regexes: [A-Za-z0-9_-]{6,64} and \\d{1,15} - closes the amplification and satisfies the bounded-quantifier contract in finding 5.

4. Add to Acceptance Criteria: 'Every video-embed path applies an exact-hostname allowlist before the ID regex' plus a negative unit test per source asserting that https://attacker.example/x?youtube.com/embed/AAAAAAAAAAA yields None.

5. Delete autoevolution_source._video_embed_url rather than injecting it; add its file/line to Task 7's 'Files to modify' rationale so the reviewer cannot miss it.

findings.title: _llm_common._encode_format_markers is an unbounded quadratic loop on the LLM-prompt path, and this feature makes it reachable from three more sources
findings.description:
This is the direct answer to 'are _MAX_TEXT_FOR_RUNS / _MAX_RUNS_PER_BLOCK still adequate' - the bounds exist in the wrong place, and the path that runs FIRST has none at all.

telegraph_publisher.py:157-158, 283-289 bounds the RENDER path: len(text) > 100000 or len(runs) > 100 logs a WARNING and falls through to plain text. _llm_common._encode_format_markers (_llm_common.py:128-176) performs structurally the same work - iterate runs, text.find(run_text) per run, sort, first-wrap-wins - with NO bound of any kind. Its only guards are 'if not runs: return text' and per-run empty/format filters. It is called from _build_user_message (_llm_common.py:239) once per patchable block per article, i.e. on the request side of every translation call.

The project's one input cap does not cover this. _PARAGRAPH_MAX_CHARS = 4000 / _truncate_paragraphs is applied to parsed['paragraphs'] - the model's RESPONSE - in all four engines (claude:434, gemini:365, openai:368, openrouter:467). Nothing truncates the outbound paragraphs, and nothing anywhere caps len(runs).

Why this feature makes it live: today only orangetrack emits bold runs. autoevolution's current _runs_from_tag is href-only (its docstring admits bold/italic are flattened), so 'bold' not in formats short-circuits the loop on every run and the scan is free. Task 7 replaces it with the shared walker, and Tasks 5 and 6 add t-hunted and lamley. After this release, three additional third-party sites feed unbounded (text, runs) pairs into an unbounded quadratic loop. The Dependencies section lists _encode_format_markers under 'Using existing (from project)' with no change and no bound; the Risks table does not mention it.
findings.location: _llm_common.py:128-176 (no bound), 210-241 (_build_user_message call site), 74-75 and 430-442 (_truncate_paragraphs applies to the RESPONSE only); telegraph_publisher.py:157-158, 283-289 (where the bounds do exist); Section: Dependencies / Using existing; Tasks 5, 6, 7
findings.impact: Availability loss on a single-process bot whose recovery is procedurally blocked. Worked example within existing fetch caps (t_hunted_source.py:52 _MAX_BYTES = 2000000; lamley_source.py:92 MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE = 5MB): a page whose body is roughly 200k repetitions of a yields one paragraph block with about 200k runs over about 200k chars of text. _encode_format_markers then performs about 200k text.find calls over a 200k-char string - on the order of 4e10 character comparisons, tens of minutes to hours of pure CPU in CPython. The bot runs one in-process daily scheduler, so the tick stalls and every remaining publication slot is missed. Per the deployment rules the operator cannot restart between 10:00 and 20:00 MSK, and all three publish slots (10:00 / 15:00 / 19:30 MSK) sit inside that window - so the stall is unrecoverable for the whole publishing day. Secondary impact: the same unbounded text is serialised into the prompt payload by json.dumps at _llm_common.py:249, so a large article inflates input_tokens without limit against a documented ~$1/day sanity threshold. Reaching this requires only a pathological or hostile page on one of three third-party blogs - no privileged access.
findings.recommendation:
Two changes, both belonging in this feature because this feature is what makes the path reachable:

1. Bound _encode_format_markers to match the renderer, sharing one constant so the two can never drift:

   # _llm_common.py - mirror telegraph_publisher's bounds
   _MAX_TEXT_FOR_MARKERS = 100_000
   _MAX_RUNS_FOR_MARKERS = 100

   def _encode_format_markers(text, runs):
       if not runs:
           return text
       if len(text) > _MAX_TEXT_FOR_MARKERS or len(runs) > _MAX_RUNS_FOR_MARKERS:
           logger.warning(
               '[markers] bound hit: text=%d runs=%d - sending unmarked',
               len(text), len(runs))
           return text          # fail-open, consistent with the renderer
       ...

2. Better: also cap at PARSE time so the oversized block never reaches SQLite or the prompt at all - see finding 3.

Add a Decision (suggest 'Decision 8: DoS bounds apply on the encode path, not only the render path') recording that the render bound sits downstream of insert_pending and of the LLM call and therefore cannot protect either. Add to Acceptance Criteria: 'No unbounded (len(runs) x len(text)) scan exists on the request path to the LLM.' Add a unit test in the Testing Strategy with about 200 runs over about 200k chars asserting the bound trips, a WARNING is logged, and the article still publishes as flat text.

findings.title: Nothing caps runs, text length, or block count at PARSE time; the removal of the heading length limit is one instance of a general gap
findings.description:
Direct answer to 'does the new heading heuristic create an unbounded input path' and 'does anything cap runs at PARSE time': the heuristic itself is not the vulnerability, but it is the visible edge of one - there is no parse-time bound anywhere in the design, and the spec twice states the absence as a positive decision. Decision 2 ends with '**No length limit.**' and its Residual risk paragraph frames a whole-bold lead paragraph purely as cosmetic ('an oversized heading ... Reversible: cosmetic, no content lost'). Decision 3b states 'No threshold on how much of an article is bold (AC7)'. Neither considers resource consumption. A whole-bold 500 KB paragraph therefore becomes a single heading block whose text is 500 KB, which is then (a) filtered, (b) persisted into the blocks JSON column, (c) serialised into the LLM prompt, and only then (d) hits telegraph_publisher's 100000-char render bound, which fails open to plain text. The one bound in the system fires after the two expensive steps. The
-splitter is a second, larger unbounded multiplier, and Decision 1 promotes it to a shared default for all four parsers. orangetrack_source.py:583-608 splits a

at every
and constructs a FRESH BeautifulSoup per segment (line 594: BeautifulSoup(f'

{seg_html}

', 'html.parser')). Segment count is uncapped, so one

containing N
costs N full parser instantiations and emits N paragraph blocks. Within lamley's 5 MB fetch cap that is on the order of 500k segments from a single tag. Today one source does this; after Tasks 5-7, four do. No per-article block cap exists either. Decision 5 caps IMAGE blocks only, and grep confirms the sole len(blocks) checks in the codebase are the LLM response-shape assertion at _llm_common.py:377 and logging. The Testing Strategy has no adversarial-size case: the unit-test list covers correctness of promotion and non-promotion but no oversized or high-cardinality input, and the Risks table's only entry for Decision 2 is the cosmetic one.
findings.location:
Section: Decisions / Decision 2 ('No length limit'), Decision 2b, Decision 3b ('No threshold on how much of an article is bold'), Decision 5 (images only); Section: Testing Strategy / Unit tests; Section: Risks (row 2); orangetrack_source.py:583-608 (
splitter, uncapped segments, per-segment BeautifulSoup); telegraph_publisher.py:283-289 (bound fires last)
findings.impact:
Three concrete degradations from one pathological or hostile source page, none of which any current control catches. (1) Memory and CPU: an uncapped
split allocates one BeautifulSoup per segment - hundreds of thousands of parser objects for a single

, within the existing 2-5 MB fetch caps. (2) Cost: an oversized block is serialised into the prompt before any bound applies, so input_tokens scale with attacker-chosen article size against a documented ~$1/day threshold. (3) Publish failure: a 500 KB

node is very likely rejected by Telegraph createPage, and because Decision 3b makes every failure silent the operator learns about it only by reading the channel. Each amplifies finding 2, since block count and run count are what feed that quadratic loop. Separately, removing the length limit is defensible on the evidence presented (286 real paragraph blocks, zero whole-bold non-headings) - the problem is not the threshold choice but that 'no limit' was decided on editorial grounds with no resource bound substituted in its place.
findings.recommendation:
Keep Decision 2's editorial rule (whole-bold AND not '.'-terminated, no EDITORIAL length limit) and add a separate defensive bound so the two concerns stay distinct: 1. In dom_blocks.py, module constants applied by BlockBuilder for all four consumers: _MAX_BLOCK_TEXT_CHARS = 20_000 # any single block's text _MAX_RUNS_PER_BLOCK = 100 # same number the renderer uses _MAX_BLOCKS_PER_ARTICLE = 500 _MAX_BR_SEGMENTS = 200 #
-splitter fan-out 2. Behaviour on trip - fail-open, matching the project's habit (promo filter, content gate, dedup gate, render bound): keep the block but drop its runs and log at WARNING; stop appending past _MAX_BLOCKS_PER_ARTICLE; past _MAX_BR_SEGMENTS emit the remainder as one block instead of splitting further. Never raise, never drop the article. 3. Do NOT gate the heading heuristic on a length bound - a 25 KB whole-bold paragraph should stay a paragraph because the block-text cap already stripped its runs, so 'entirely covered by bold runs' is no longer true. That makes the two rules compose instead of arguing. 4. Reuse the existing splitter instead of one soup per segment: BeautifulSoup(...) once, then operate on the tree, or build all segments in a single parse. 5. Add to Acceptance Criteria: 'No block emitted by any parser exceeds _MAX_BLOCK_TEXT_CHARS or _MAX_RUNS_PER_BLOCK; no article exceeds _MAX_BLOCKS_PER_ARTICLE.' Add adversarial unit tests to Task 1's list: a 500 KB whole-bold paragraph, a

with 10000
, and a paragraph with 5000 spans - asserting bounds trip, WARNING logged, article still publishes.

findings.title: The img-src scheme allowlist becomes a per-site injected callable with no stated contract, and the publisher validates nothing of its own
findings.description:
The same structural flaw as finding 1, on the second of the three injected callables. Decision 1 names 'image-src picker' as injected and states no contract about scheme or host validation, so whatever each site supplies becomes the sole enforcement point. The four candidate implementations are not equivalent:

- orangetrack (_best_img_src, orangetrack_source.py:451-487) routes every candidate through _safe_img_src (:233-248): rejects non-string, scheme-relative //evil/x, and any scheme outside {http, https}. This is the strong one, and its docstring states the project's principle explicitly - 'defense-in-depth - Telegraph filters too, but the parser must not emit them in the first place'.
- t_hunted (:228-243) and lamley (:406-419) use src.startswith('http') plus _is_blogger_image_url host checks.
- autoevolution (:200-214) uses only (href or '').startswith('http') and candidate.startswith('http'). That is a prefix test, not a scheme test: 'httpx://evil/x.jpg'.startswith('http') is True. Worse, its gallery path (:320-331) applies no scheme test at all - the only filter is gallery_href_re.search(href) where gallery_href_re = re.compile(r'/gallery/[^"\']*' + re.escape(slug)). Because that is an unanchored search over the full href, an absolute URL on any host (https://attacker.example/gallery/<slug>.jpg, or even javascript:x/gallery/<slug>) matches and is appended verbatim as {'type':'image','src': href}.

And telegraph_publisher._build_content_from_blocks re-validates nothing: figure_img at :386-390 emits {'tag':'img','attrs':{'src': src}} and iframe at :392 emits {'tag':'iframe','attrs':{'src': src}} straight from the block. It trusts its callers absolutely. Today that is orangetrack (safe) plus autoevolution (weak). Tasks 5 and 6 add two more block producers, and Decision 5 explicitly designates this function 'the single choke point every source passes through' for the image cap - a choke point that performs no validation is the natural place to add one.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 1 (image-src picker as injected callable), Decision 5 ('the single choke point'); Task 7; telegraph_publisher.py:386-392 and 400-410 (zero validation); autoevolution_source.py:200-214, 320-331; orangetrack_source.py:233-248, 451-487; t_hunted_source.py:228-243; lamley_source.py:406-419
findings.impact: The parser emits img/iframe src values the project's own stated policy forbids it to emit. Currently absorbed by two downstream layers - Telegraph's createPage validator on the published page, and preview_renderer's ^https?:// check plus CSP default-src 'none' on the local file:// preview - so this is a defence-in-depth failure rather than a live XSS. But both absorbers are outside this codebase's control (a Telegraph validator change silently un-protects every source at once), and the local preview is exactly the surface preview_renderer's module docstring says it hardened 'against XSS from a compromised upstream article' under the strongly-trusted file:// origin. The concrete reachable outcome today is hot-linking attacker-hosted images into the published Telegraph page (tracking pixels that deanonymise every channel reader, or bait-and-switch image swaps after publication) via autoevolution's unanchored gallery match. Formalising the weakest picker as an injected value means the next source added inherits whichever example it copies.
findings.recommendation:
1. Make the scheme allowlist a non-negotiable floor inside dom_blocks.py rather than a per-site concern. Move _safe_href / _safe_img_src / _ALLOWED_HREF_SCHEMES / _ALLOWED_IMG_SCHEMES into dom_blocks.py and have BlockBuilder.emit_image apply safe_img_src to whatever the injected picker returns. The injected callable then chooses WHICH candidate (srcset vs src vs lightbox <a href>) - a presentation decision - while the module decides whether it is emittable at all.

2. Add defence in depth at the choke point Decision 5 already identifies:

   # telegraph_publisher._build_content_from_blocks
   def figure_img(src, caption=''):
       if not _safe_media_url(src):        # ^https?:// only
           return None                     # skip the block entirely
       ...

   and the same for iframe(src). Skip-and-log rather than raise, consistent with the module's existing fail-open style.

3. Anchor autoevolution's gallery match so it cannot accept a foreign host: require the href to pass safe_img_src AND resolve to an autoevolution host, and anchor the pattern (re.compile(r'^/images/news/gallery/...') against the parsed path, not re.search over the whole URL).

4. Replace every startswith('http') in t_hunted, lamley and autoevolution with the shared helper - a prefix test is not a scheme test.

5. Add to Acceptance Criteria: 'No parser emits an image or video src outside {http, https}; _build_content_from_blocks independently drops any src that fails the scheme allowlist.' Add a negative unit test per source for javascript:, data:, file: and scheme-relative //evil/x.jpg.

findings.title: The ReDoS / bounded-quantifier contract is asserted in the audit task but stated nowhere the implementer will read it
findings.description:
Task 10 instructs the auditor to check 'the ReDoS-safety contract the project requires of all parser regex (bounded quantifiers only)'. That contract appears in exactly one other place in the repository - .claude/skills/project-knowledge/references/patterns.md:123, scoped to boilerplate_filter: 'keep length-bounded (_MAX_BOILERPLATE_LEN = 120) and anchored at ^. ReDoS-safe - no nested greedy quantifiers.' It appears nowhere in the tech-spec's Architecture, Decisions, Testing Strategy or Acceptance Criteria, and nowhere in Task 1 - the task that actually creates dom_blocks.py. Nor is it in user-spec.md, which contains no security content at all (grep for redos/security/allowlist/scheme/SSRF/XSS/sanitiz/DoS/inject returns nothing).

So the obligation exists only in the audit that runs AFTER the code is written, which inverts the intended order: Task 10 will discover violations that Task 1 was never told to avoid.

On the substance, I found no true catastrophic backtracking in what is being moved - _text_from_runs uses re.sub(r'\\s+', ' ', ...) (orangetrack_source.py:283), a single character class with no nested group, so it is linear. But three regexes in the code being consolidated are open-ended and therefore violate the contract as Task 10 words it ('bounded quantifiers only', i.e. {1,N}): orangetrack _YOUTUBE_ID_RE ([A-Za-z0-9_-]{6,}, orangetrack_source.py:88-91), autoevolution YOUTUBE_ID_RE ([A-Za-z0-9_-]+) and VIMEO_ID_RE (\\d+) (autoevolution_source.py:33-37). Their real cost is unbounded capture length (see finding 1) rather than backtracking.

There is also an unspecified new regex. Decision 2's rule requires testing trailing punctuation - '.' disqualifies, while '...' and '....' and '?' and '!' qualify. The spec does not say how, and a plausible-looking implementation with a leading .* or a nested alternation over a 500 KB heading (finding 3 shows such headings are permitted) is where a genuine ReDoS would be introduced.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 1; Task 1; Task 10; Section: Acceptance Criteria; orangetrack_source.py:88-91, 283; autoevolution_source.py:33-37; .claude/skills/project-knowledge/references/patterns.md:123
findings.impact: The extraction is the one moment when all four parsers' regexes pass through a single reviewer, and the spec spends that moment without stating the constraint. Concretely: the open-ended ID captures survive into shared code and gain three more callers (finding 1's amplification path), and the unspecified heading-punctuation regex is written with no guidance while operating on inputs the spec has explicitly declined to length-limit. A backtracking regex on this path stalls the single-process bot exactly as finding 2 describes, with the same 10:00-20:00 MSK restart bar.
findings.recommendation:
1. Add an explicit invariant to Architecture (or a short 'Security invariants preserved' subsection - see finding 9): 'Every regex in dom_blocks.py uses bounded quantifiers ({1,N}) and is anchored where the input shape allows. No nested quantifier over a group. Every capture that becomes part of an emitted URL or block text is length-bounded.'

2. Add it to Task 1's description so the implementer sees it, and to Acceptance Criteria as a checkable line: '[ ] Every regex in dom_blocks.py uses bounded quantifiers; a test asserts no pattern contains + or * applied to a group.'

3. Bound the three existing patterns while they are being consolidated: [A-Za-z0-9_-]{6,64}, \\d{1,15}.

4. Specify the heading-punctuation test as string operations, not a regex, which removes the risk entirely:

   _HEADING_OK_SUFFIXES = ('...', '\u2026', '\u2026.', '?', '!')
   def _is_sentence_terminated(text):
       t = text.rstrip()
       if t.endswith(_HEADING_OK_SUFFIXES):
           return False
       return t.endswith('.')

5. Add a Testing Strategy line: 'Each dom_blocks regex is timed against a 1 MB adversarial input and must complete in under 100 ms.'

findings.title: Kill switch defaults ON for a feature the spec itself says cannot be verified before deploy, while every failure mode is silent and the switch cannot be flipped during the publishing day
findings.description:
Asked directly: no, default ON is not the safe default here. Four statements in this same spec combine against it.

1. Decision 6: 'One env flag, default ON'. Default ON means the flag's ABSENCE from the prod .env enables the feature - nobody has to consciously turn it on, and the deploy that ships the code is the deploy that activates it on live third-party HTML.
2. Testing Strategy / E2E tests: 'None. E2E would require live fetches; autoevolution article pages return 403 to our client ... and lamley is throttled 20 s + 24 h blacklist. The operator's side-by-side comparison after deploy is the E2E substitute.' The spec states plainly that the first real exercise of this code on real pages happens in production.
3. Decision 3b: 'Every failure mode in this feature degrades to flat text without pinging the operator.' The only signal anywhere is the AC8 count-mismatch WARNING in a log the operator reads over ssh on request.
4. Deploys are barred 10:00-20:00 MSK (Task 13 explains why: job() runs immediately on container start), and all three publish slots (10:00 / 15:00 / 19:30 MSK) fall inside that window. Flipping the flag off requires an env change plus a container restart - i.e. the mitigation is unavailable for the whole ten-hour period during which every publication carries the defect.

The spec leans on this switch as a control it cannot actually exercise in time. Decision 2's Residual risk says the oversized-heading case is 'covered by the kill switch and the operator's post-deploy check', and the Risks table repeats 'Kill switch + operator's post-deploy read' - but detection is a human reading the channel and remediation is a barred restart.

The project has already made this exact decision the other way. news_bot.py:138-152 carries both idioms side by side and the comment on the newer, safety-relevant one is explicit: 'CRITICAL, deliberately INVERTED default vs DEDUP_SERIES_ENABLED: this flag is OFF unless the env var is an explicit on-word (1/true/yes/on, case-insensitive); unset / blank / anything else -> disabled. Prod-only opt-in'. Decision 6 says it will reuse 'the same truthy/falsy word set as the existing two' - it copies the parsing but picks the riskier of the two defaults, and gives no reason for choosing DEDUP_SERIES_ENABLED's default over REVIEW_BUTTONS_ENABLED's.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 6 (default ON), Decision 2 Residual risk, Decision 2b, Decision 3b; Section: Testing Strategy / E2E tests; Section: Risks (rows 2 and 4); Task 3; Task 13; news_bot.py:134-137 (DEDUP_SERIES_ENABLED, default ON) vs 138-152 (REVIEW_BUTTONS_ENABLED, deliberately default OFF, fail-closed)
findings.impact: Default ON is the multiplier that converts every other finding here from a bug into a production incident of unbounded duration. On the first tick after deploy, three parsers begin walking live third-party HTML through brand-new shared code, with no pre-deploy E2E, no ping on any failure, and no ability to disable until after 20:00 MSK. Findings 1, 2, 3 and 4 all reach production through this door: a CPU stall (finding 2) takes out the whole publishing day, an oversized heading (finding 3) fails createPage silently, an unsafe or attacker-hosted src (findings 1 and 4) is published to the channel. Note the asymmetry with Task 13's own care - the spec reasons carefully about restart timing for the deploy itself, then relies on a restart-gated switch as its safety control.
findings.recommendation:
1. Invert the default to OFF and follow the REVIEW_BUTTONS_ENABLED idiom the project already documents as the fail-closed one:

   # dom_blocks.py - const<->env name identity, same as the existing two
   BLOCKS_FORMATTING_ENABLED = os.getenv(
       'BLOCKS_FORMATTING_ENABLED', ''
   ).strip().lower() in ('1', 'true', 'yes', 'on')

   Read it as a module attribute at call time (not captured at import) so tests can monkeypatch and the operator can flip it via env plus restart - exactly the pattern news_bot.py:131-133 documents.

2. Amend Decision 6 with the rationale: default OFF because no pre-deploy E2E exists (Testing Strategy), all failures are silent (Decision 3b), and the switch cannot be flipped 10:00-20:00 MSK.

3. Change the rollout in Task 13 / Task 14 to a staged enable outside the window: deploy with the flag OFF, confirm no regression against the flat-text baseline, then set the flag and restart outside the window, then run Task 14's per-source checks. This also makes the -0.10% / -1.18% flag-off drift measurable in production rather than only in the research script.

4. Amend the two Risks rows and Decision 2's Residual risk to stop crediting the kill switch with mitigation it cannot deliver inside the publishing window; state the real exposure (up to one publishing day) or add the runtime bounds from finding 3 as the actual mitigation.

5. Update the Acceptance Criteria line 'Flag off => no blocks emitted by any of the three parsers' to also assert the DEFAULT: '[ ] With the env var unset, no blocks are emitted (default OFF).' As written that criterion passes under either default, so it does not pin the decision.

findings.category: A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.title: No observable signal on the new untrusted-input path: nothing counts heuristic promotions or cap trips
findings.description:
Decision 3b makes degradation 'silent and unconditional' and rules out pings for unparsable markup (AC5), dropped markers (AC6) and bold-heaviness (AC7); only the AC8 count mismatch logs a WARNING. Suppressing PINGS for cosmetic outcomes is a reasonable operator call and I am not disputing it - the gap is that the spec provides no LOGGING either, and no counters, so there is no way to notice a source page starting to behave pathologically.

The surrounding code does log at this granularity: telegraph_publisher.py:284-288 logs the DoS bound trip, :243-246 logs unbalanced ** stripping, _llm_common.py:436-441 logs paragraph truncation, orangetrack_source.py:1069 logs the empty-embed fallback. The new module is specified with none of that. Concretely there is no log line when the heading heuristic promotes a paragraph (so nobody can tell whether the measured 24-promotions-per-286-blocks rate still holds in production - which the Agent Verification Plan says it wants to confirm), nor when any of the bounds recommended in findings 2 and 3 would trip.

Related: the Agent Verification Plan proposes re-running the code-research.md measurement script against live t-hunted articles to confirm the heuristic 'still scores as measured'. That is a good check, but it is a one-off at deploy time; production drift after that is unobservable.
findings.location: Section: Decisions / Decision 3b; Section: Agent Verification Plan; Task 8; compare telegraph_publisher.py:243-246, 284-288; _llm_common.py:436-441
findings.impact: Detection for findings 1-4 in production is 'the operator reads the channel'. A source page that begins producing 300-block articles, 50 KB headings, or video embeds from non-YouTube hosts produces no log line, so the condition persists until a human notices a visibly wrong post. This is also what makes finding 6's default-ON exposure open-ended: without a signal, nobody knows to flip the switch.
findings.recommendation:
Keep Decision 3b's no-ping rule and add one sentence distinguishing pings from logs: 'Silent means no operator ping. Every degradation still logs at WARNING (or DEBUG for routine heuristic decisions) so the condition is diagnosable from docker logs.'

Specify in Task 1: one summary DEBUG/INFO line per article from BlockBuilder - blocks emitted, heading promotions, runs total, max block text length - and a WARNING whenever any bound from finding 3 trips, naming the source. That makes the post-deploy check in Task 14 ('no WARNING about a blocks/paragraphs mismatch in the logs') extend naturally to the new bounds at zero extra operator cost, and makes the heuristic's production promotion rate greppable instead of requiring the research script to be re-run.

findings.title: Literal ** in scraped source text is not escaped before entering the marker round-trip, now on four sources instead of one
findings.description:
On the question of new injection surface from sharing the walker: the LLM-prompt path is largely unchanged, because scraped article text already reaches the prompt today as flat paragraphs - blocks add no new channel for attacker-controlled prose, and prompt injection against the transcreation model is a pre-existing property of the design, not something this feature introduces. Existing guards are decent: _llm_common.py:377 rejects a response whose block count differs from expected_block_count, telegraph_publisher.py:310-313 allowlists format names against _FORMAT_TAGS and drops unknown values, :396-398 clamps heading level to (3,4), href rendering is disabled outright at :308, block type dispatch is a closed if/elif, and preview_renderer escapes everything and allowlists tags, schemes and attribute names.

The one genuinely new detail is the ** marker syntax. _encode_format_markers (_llm_common.py:128-176) wraps bold spans in ** without escaping ** that the source text already contained, and _decode_format_markers (:187-208) parses ** out of the response without distinguishing model-authored from source-authored markers. So a source paragraph containing a literal ** produces ambiguous markers in the prompt. Blast radius is cosmetic and bounded - _BOLD_MARKER_RE forbids newlines in the body so a stray marker cannot swallow a paragraph, _decode_bold_markers (telegraph_publisher.py:242-247) strips unbalanced leftovers with a WARNING rather than publishing them, and source runs outrank model guesses. This feature widens it from one source emitting bold runs to four.
findings.location: _llm_common.py:128-176 (encode, no escaping), 184-208 (decode); telegraph_publisher.py:195-198, 242-247; Section: Dependencies / Using existing; Tasks 5, 6, 7
findings.impact: Wrong emphasis on published text: a source paragraph containing literal ** can produce a bold span the author never wrote, or suppress one they did. No XSS, no code execution, no data exposure - the render path allowlists formats and the preview escapes all text. Filed because it is a correctness edge on a newly widened untrusted-input path and it interacts with the Task 11 note about one-sided invariants ('bold appears' tests that miss 'bold appears where it should not').
findings.recommendation: Add a Testing Strategy case to Task 1's dom_blocks list and to Task 8's integration list: a source paragraph containing a literal ** survives the parser -> encode -> LLM -> decode -> render round-trip without gaining or losing emphasis. If it does not, escape source-origin ** in _encode_format_markers (for example to \\*\\*) and unescape after decode. This is also the natural negative control Task 11 is asking for.

findings.title: Neither spec contains any security content, which is the root cause of findings 1, 4 and 5
findings.description:
user-spec.md contains no security material at all (grep for redos, security, безопасность, allowlist, scheme, SSRF, XSS, sanitize, DoS, inject returns nothing). tech-spec.md mentions security only in Task 10's own description and in one Task 3 reviewer slot. Architecture, Decisions 1-7, Data Models, Dependencies, Testing Strategy, Risks and Acceptance Criteria contain none.

This matters more than usual for this particular change. The feature relocates every parser-level input-validation gate the project has - href scheme allowlist, img scheme allowlist, YouTube host allowlist, chrome-class suppression - out of the module that currently owns them and behind an injection interface. The spec's one hard acceptance gate is behavioural equivalence ('orangetrack_source tests pass without any test file being edited'), which is a good gate for OUTPUT but silent on invariants: a rewrite that drops _safe_href's // check or reorders the host gate after the ID regex can still produce byte-identical output on all 14 sampled articles, because none of them exercise the hostile input those guards exist for.

Task 10 is scheduled in the Audit Wave, i.e. after Tasks 1-8 are written. That is the wrong order for invariant preservation: the audit will find omissions the implementer was never told to avoid, and by then four parsers depend on the seam.

One related observation on Decision 1's seam choice. The rationale for injecting callables is per-site behaviour, but two of the three injected values are security controls (image-src picker, video-embed wrapper) and only one is genuinely presentational (chrome-class predicate). Injecting a security control is what makes findings 1 and 4 possible. Injecting DATA - allowed hosts, chrome markers, candidate-attribute preference - while the module keeps the enforcement gives the same flexibility without the hazard.
findings.location: Section: Architecture; Section: Decisions (all); Section: Acceptance Criteria; Task 1; Task 10; work/source-formatting-parity/user-spec.md (no security content)
findings.impact: No implementer of Tasks 1 or 7 is told that _safe_href, _safe_img_src and the pre-regex YouTube host gate are load-bearing, so silently dropping one passes every stated gate: orangetrack's tests assert output shape on benign fixtures, and the 14-article measurement contains no hostile input. Findings 1, 4 and 5 are three instances of this single omission.
findings.recommendation:
1. Add a short 'Security invariants preserved' subsection to Architecture, listed as checkable items rather than prose: - _safe_href: schemes limited to {http, https, mailto}; scheme-relative // rejected; unsafe href degrades the anchor to plain text (never drops the text). - _safe_img_src / video src: {http, https} only, enforced by dom_blocks regardless of what a per-site picker returns. - Every video-embed path: exact-hostname allowlist BEFORE the ID regex (finding 1). - All dom_blocks regex: bounded quantifiers, bounded captures (finding 5). - Parse-time bounds on block text, runs per block, blocks per article,
segments (finding 3). - Encode-path DoS bound mirroring the render-path bound (finding 2). 2. Mirror each as an Acceptance Criteria checkbox so pre-deploy QA (Task 12) verifies them instead of only the behavioural gate. 3. Narrow Decision 1's seam: inject DATA (allowed-host tuples, chrome markers, candidate-attribute preference), keep ENFORCEMENT in dom_blocks. Record it as an amendment to Decision 1 with findings 1 and 4 as the reason. 4. Move the security review earlier: add 'security-auditor' to Task 1's reviewer list (it is currently only on Task 3), so the module that owns all four gates is reviewed when it is written rather than in the Audit Wave after three consumers depend on it. 5. Note for the orchestrator: tech-spec.md was modified during this review (Decisions 2b and 3b appeared mid-run; reviewed state is mtime 2026-07-30 11:54:23Z, 458 lines). Re-check findings 3 and 6 against the current text if it has moved again - Decision 2b changes which sources the heuristic applies to but not the absence of any bound on it.
